title: דִּי clauses

objectives.can: Decide what דִּי is doing: relative, genitive, 'that' after verbs of knowing and saying, purpose, or cause.

explanation.summary: דִּי is the hinge of Aramaic subordination. By itself it is relative ('who, which'), genitive ('of') or 'that'. After a preposition it makes a conjunction: 'until', 'when', 'because'. The word does not change, so you decide what it is doing from what stands before it and what follows it.

sections.heading: Ask two questions
body: The first lesson on particles said that דִּי has several jobs. This lesson teaches you how to choose. Ask: what comes just before דִּי, and what comes just after it?

If a noun comes before it and a verb clause follows, it is a relative. If a noun comes before it and another noun follows with no verb, it is a genitive, 'of'. If a verb of knowing, seeing, saying or informing comes before it, it means 'that'. If a preposition or a word like כָּל קֳבֵל comes before it, the pair is a conjunction. If an imperfect verb follows and the sense is aim, it is purpose.

sections.heading: The relative, with and without a pronoun
body: A relative clause says something about the noun before it. In English the relative word does the work of a pronoun inside the clause: 'the men whom you appointed'. Aramaic often adds a pronoun to say the same thing again. In Daniel 3:12 the Chaldeans speak of גֻּבְרִין יְהוּדָאיִן דִּי מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן: 'Jewish men whom you appointed' with, in the clause, יָתְהוֹן, 'them'. The pronoun repeats the noun and you do not translate it.

But the pronoun is not always there. In the same verse the Chaldeans mention לְצֶלֶם דַּהֲבָא דִּי הֲקֵימְתָּ, the golden image 'that you set up', and here nothing repeats the image. Compare Daniel 6:17, where the king says אֱלָהָךְ דִּי אַנְתְּ פָּלַח לֵהּ, 'your God whom you serve', with לֵהּ, 'him', repeating 'God'; and Daniel 3:17, where the three friends say אֱלָהַנָא דִּי אֲנַחְנָא פָלְחִין, 'our God whom we serve', with no pronoun. The two ways say the same thing. When a pronoun is there, do not take it as a new person.

A relative may also stand without a noun before it. In Daniel 3:6 וּמַן דִּי לָא יִפֵּל וְיִסְגֻּד means 'and whoever does not fall down and worship'. In Daniel 5:21 וּלְמַן דִּי יִצְבֵּה is 'and to whomever he wishes'.

sections.heading: Of, that, and what was said
body: Between two nouns דִּי is 'of': רֵאשָׁה דִּי דַהֲבָא, 'its head of gold' (Daniel 2:38), or לְגֻבָּא דִּי אַרְיָוָתָא, 'into the den of lions' (Daniel 6:17). The same pair of nouns could be joined by the construct state; דִּי is the other way to do it. After a noun, דִּי can also begin a phrase with no verb, as in בֵּית אֱלָהָא דִּי בִירוּשְׁלֶם (Ezra 5:2): 'the house of God that is in Jerusalem'. English has to choose between 'of' and 'which is'; the Aramaic does not.

After a verb of knowing, seeing, hearing or informing, דִּי introduces what is known. In Daniel 2:8 the king says יָדַע אֲנָה דִּי, 'I know that'. In Daniel 3:18 the friends say יְדִיעַ לֶהֱוֵא לָךְ מַלְכָּא דִּי, 'let it be known to you, O king, that'. In Daniel 5:14 the king says to Daniel וְשִׁמְעֵת עֲלָךְ דִּי, 'I have heard about you that'. Any tense may follow this 'that'.

After a verb of saying, דִּי can also open the very words that were spoken, like opening quotation marks. In Daniel 6:6 the plotters are אָמְרִין דִּי לָא נְהַשְׁכַּח לְדָנִיֵּאל, and what follows is in the first person plural (נְהַשְׁכַּח, 'we shall find'): they are quoting themselves. The person of the verb after דִּי tells you whether the words are reported or quoted.

sections.heading: Aim, reason and time
body: For purpose, דִּי is followed by an imperfect, and often by לָא. In Daniel 6:18 the king seals the stone with the rings so that nothing may change: דִּי לָא תִשְׁנֵא. In Daniel 4:14 עַד דִּבְרַת דִּי יִנְדְּעוּן means 'to the end that they may know'. Compare the 'that' of knowing: purpose looks forward to something intended, the other 'that' reports something already known or said.

For a reason, Aramaic uses the three-word phrase כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי, 'because', 'inasmuch as'. In Daniel 5:12 the queen gives the reason for sending for Daniel: 'because an extraordinary spirit was found in him'. Treat the three words as one conjunction. The shorter לָקֳבֵל דִּי does the same in Ezra 6:13.

A preposition plus דִּי makes a conjunction of time. עַד דִּי is 'until' or 'while': חָזֵה הֲוַיְתָ עַד דִּי הִתְגְּזֶרֶת אֶבֶן in Daniel 2:34 is 'you were looking until a stone was cut out'. כְּדִי is 'when': וְדָנִיֵּאל כְּדִי יְדַע in Daniel 6:11 is 'and Daniel, when he knew'. מִן דִּי is 'after' or 'once' in Ezra 4:23: 'when the copy of the letter had been read'. Learn these as whole words.

misunderstandings: A pronoun inside a relative clause is not a new character. In גֻּבְרִין יְהוּדָאיִן דִּי מַנִּיתָ יָתְהוֹן the word יָתְהוֹן only repeats 'the men'; in English you translate 'the men whom you appointed'.
דִּי does not tell you its job by itself. The same word is relative in Daniel 3:12 and genitive in Daniel 2:38: look at what comes before and after.
Two דִּי in a row do two different jobs. In Daniel 2:8 כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי חֲזֵיתוֹן דִּי אַזְדָּא מִנִּי מִלְּתָא the first is part of 'because' and the second is 'that'.
Not every 'that' is the same word. The 'that' of knowing (יָדַע אֲנָה דִּי) is not the demonstrative 'that' (דָּךְ or דְּנָה), which points at a thing.

deeper.heading: How one word became many
body: Grammarians trace the conjunctions and the 'that' of דִּי back to the relative. A phrase like 'until that' is 'until the time that', and 'because' is built from a word meaning 'in front of' and 'that'. In the texts you will see the pattern repeat: a preposition (עַד, כְּ, מִן, קֳבֵל) before דִּי gives a conjunction. Whether a given דִּי is 'that' or 'because' is sometimes a matter of judgment, and translators differ in a few verses.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The first דִּי begins a relative clause about the 'Jewish men'; the pronoun יָתְהוֹן repeats them inside the clause. The second דִּי, near the end, begins a relative clause about the image: דִּי הֲקֵימְתָּ, 'that you set up', with no repeating pronoun.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then the king commanded, and they brought Daniel, and cast him into the den of lions. Now the king spoke and said unto Daniel: 'Thy God whom thou servest continually, He will deliver thee.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The first דִּי links two nouns: 'the den of lions'. The second begins a relative clause about 'your God', and לֵהּ repeats him inside it: 'whom you serve'.

examples.analysis: After יָדַע אֲנָה, 'I know', the first דִּי means 'that'. כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי is 'because'. The next דִּי means 'that' again, after 'you see'.

quoted.english: Then when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power.

check.explain: The clause that follows (the copy of the letter was read) is the earlier event; the main verb, 'they went', comes later.

reading.why: The king's answer and the Chaldeans' reply use almost every job of דִּי: 'that' after a verb of knowing, 'because' with כָּל קֳבֵל דִּי, 'until' with עַד דִּי, a relative with and without a pronoun, and a relative clause on 'no one' with לָא אִיתַי.
